content.text:
There are two separate degradations in the window (2025-08-19, ~06:37–06:41 UTC), and they affect different endpoints. The first one produces the hard failures; the second produces the slow requests.

## Affected endpoints

**1. Hard failures: dashboard consign endpoints (06:37–06:39)**
- `ts-ui-dashboard` returned 503 on `GET /api/v1/consignservice/consigns/account/{id}` (113 spans) and `.../consigns/order/{id}` (7 spans). The loadgenerator saw the same 503s, about 8 s each.
- Normal traffic has zero 5xx. In the abnormal window, 100 of 112 dashboard consign requests failed at 06:38. By 06:39 they were back to about 16 ms with no errors.

**2. Slow requests: travel-planning and preserve chain (06:40 onward)**
- User-facing latency roughly doubled or tripled. Examples from the loadgenerator's view: travelPlan/cheapest averages 1710 ms vs 670 ms normal, preserve 924 ms vs 336 ms, travelservice/trips/left 733 ms vs 188 ms.
- No 5xx errors in this phase.

## Root cause 1: ts-consign-service CPU burst (high confidence)

- The consign pod (`ts-consign-service-6cfc6565f6-fphwj`) hit CPU limit utilization of 0.437 average and 0.871 max at 06:38. Normal averages 0.014 with a max of 0.11.
- JVM CPU time jumped to 139.6 at 06:39 (normal max 14.8). Memory and thread count stayed flat.
- Consign request volume was lower than normal, so this is per-request cost, not load.
- DB client spans stayed around 1 ms. The time was in the controller: `ConsignController.findByAccountId` averaged 34 ms with a max of 714 ms, and `updateConsign` averaged 521 ms. The process itself was burning CPU, not waiting on its database.
- Propagation: consign → `ts-ui-dashboard` (503 after its consign call fails) → loadgenerator (503).
- The burst ended by 06:39, which explains why the failures are short-lived.

## Root cause 2: CPU-bound self-time degradation in the travel-planning chain (medium confidence on the origin)

From 06:40 onward, these services show higher CPU and slower controller work, while their database spans stay fast (~2 ms vs ~0.5 ms normal):

| Service | Pod CPU (pre → post 06:40) | Controller self-time (normal → abnormal) |
|---|---|---|
| ts-seat-service | 0.207 → 0.506 | `getLeftTicketOfInterval` 21 → 64 ms; `SeatController.create` 17 → 149 ms |
| ts-basic-service | 0.145 → 0.428 | `queryForTravel` 44 → 128 ms |
| ts-route-service | 0.096 → 0.327 | Slow mainly when called from basic |
| ts-travel-service | 0.146 → 0.284 | Callee latency rose for every caller |
| ts-travel2-service | 0.085 → 0.13 | Callee latency rose |
| ts-route-plan-service | 0.041 → 0.083 | Callee latency rose |

- The degradation is in the callee's own processing. Caller-side client durations match the callee's server durations, so transport is not the problem.
- **Origin (most likely): ts-seat-service.** It shows the largest self-time jump among the chain and is slow for every caller (travel, travel2, travel-plan, preserve). Its pod CPU rose about 2.4x.
- **Co-degraded: ts-basic-service.** It shows a similar self-time and CPU jump and is slow for travel, travel2, and preserve. I can't tell from this telemetry whether it is an independent second origin or is being driven by the same load shift.
- ts-route-service and ts-travel-service look like victims. Their own work is only modestly slower, and the latency they show is mostly inherited from callers.
- Node-level CPU stays low, and the affected pods are spread across worker1, worker3, and worker6, so this is not a single noisy node.
- Logs in this phase contain only baseline noise: "Cookie not found" warnings, seat "No content" warnings, and food-service and RabbitMQ errors that also appear in normal traffic.

## Propagation and summary

- Fault A (consign CPU burst, 06:37–06:39) → ts-ui-dashboard 503s on consign endpoints → loadgenerator 503s.
- Fault B (seat, possibly with basic, from 06:40 onward) → travel-service, travel2-service, route-plan-service, travel-plan-service, and preserve-service latency → user-facing slowness on travelPlan, preserve, and trips endpoints.

## Gaps and caveats

- Trace stitching is incomplete. In the slow travel-plan example, the route-service span does not hang under the travel-plan client span, so I could not confirm the exact callee of every slow POST.
- Hubble edge-latency metrics are all NaN, so they could not be used.
- I could not determine why seat (and possibly basic) began consuming more CPU at 06:40. The telemetry shows the effect but not its trigger.
